opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back. It's a great question, and I want to separate two things: what a moratorium would do *if* it held, and how likely it is to hold.

If you could get a genuinely global, well-enforced pause, I think it could make a large difference to the probability of AGI by 2040. A lot of the recent progress has come from scaling: bigger training runs, more compute, more investment. That's actually one of the more governable parts of the picture. Frontier training runs need enormous data centers and specialized chips made by a handful of companies in a handful of countries. So unlike many dangerous technologies, there's a physical chokepoint here. A moratorium focused on very large training runs could slow things substantially, perhaps pushing the arrival date back by years, which matters a lot if those years are spent on alignment research and building institutions.

But I'd be cautious about overstating it. A few things cut the other way. First, algorithmic progress continues even if compute is capped. Researchers keep finding ways to get more capability out of the same hardware, so a pause on scale isn't a pause on progress. Second, there's the "compute overhang" worry: if chips keep getting cheaper and algorithms keep improving during a pause, then when it ends you might get a sudden jump rather than gradual progress, and that could be worse from a safety perspective. Third, enforcement. "Global" is doing a lot of work in the phrase "global moratorium." If major players stay outside it, or comply in letter but not spirit, the effect shrinks and you may simply shift who gets there first.

So my rough view is that a moratorium is neither a silver bullet nor pointless. A well-designed one could meaningfully lower the chance of AGI by 2040. I'd value it less for the delay itself than for what you do with the delay. The point of buying time is to spend it: on technical safety work, on verification regimes, and on reaching the kind of international agreement that lets us go forward carefully rather than racing. If a pause just postpones the same reckless race by a few years, we haven't gained much. If it changes the character of how humanity approaches this transition, that could be one of the most valuable things we ever do.

r001.rationale: The response says a well-enforced moratorium could meaningfully lower the chance of AGI by 2040, but it does not indicate that it could create at least a 10% chance AGI is not achieved by then.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it depends enormously on what kind of moratorium we're talking about, and I'd want to separate a few things out.

If you imagine a genuinely global, enforced moratorium — something more like the kind of coordination we've seen on, say, human cloning or certain classes of weapons — then the direct effect on the probability of AGI by 2040 is obviously to lower it, and perhaps lower it a great deal. The frontier labs are the ones pushing the compute scaling, and if you stop the largest training runs, you remove the main engine driving timelines forward. So in that world I'd expect the chance of AGI by 2040 to drop substantially, maybe by more than half, depending on how long the pause lasts and how it ends.

But I don't think that's really the interesting question, because I'm sceptical that a moratorium of that kind is achievable in the near term. What's more realistic is a partial or leaky one — some countries or some companies pausing, others continuing. And there the effect is much more ambiguous. You might slow the leaders while doing very little about the overall trajectory, and you could end up shifting development towards actors who are less careful, which is a worse outcome than if you'd never paused at all. So the effect on timelines might be modest, and the effect on safety could even be negative.

The other thing I'd stress is that a moratorium doesn't freeze the world. Algorithmic progress continues, hardware continues to improve, and a lot of research can be done at scales below whatever threshold you set. So when a pause ends, you may find that capabilities jump quite sharply because all of that latent progress gets realised at once. That's sometimes called a compute overhang, and it's a real concern. It means the probability by 2040 might fall less than you'd naively expect — you've delayed things, but you've also set up a more abrupt transition.

Where I come out is that I'm more interested in slowing things than stopping them. The underlying question I care about is whether humanity gets to a position where we understand these systems well enough to make the transition safely. A moratorium is one tool for buying that time, but it's a blunt one. I'd rather see things like compute governance, verification regimes, and international agreements on what kinds of training runs require oversight — mechanisms that could, if needed, scale up into something like a pause but don't require us to get full global agreement from day one.

So to put a number on it, if you asked me what a realistic moratorium does to the chance of AGI by 2040, I'd say it probably reduces it somewhat, but I wouldn't be confident it moves it by more than, say, ten or twenty percentage points, and I'd be more concerned with what it does to the shape of the transition than to the date.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a realistic moratorium would probably reduce the chance of AGI by 2040 by 10–20 percentage points, clearly supporting at least a 10% chance that it would not be achieved by then.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it could make a substantial difference, but a lot depends on what we mean by a global moratorium. Is it an agreement that most countries sign up to, or is it something that’s effectively monitored and enforced? And how long does it last?

A durable, well-enforced moratorium would reduce the chance of reaching AGI by 2040, potentially quite dramatically. But I wouldn’t treat it as making that chance zero. There could be violations, or progress in algorithms could make it possible to build such systems with much less computing power, which might make enforcement harder.

There’s also a distinction between delaying AGI and making its eventual development safer. A pause could give us time to work on safety and governance, but we’d have to actually use that time well. So I’d want to know both how much development it would prevent and what we would do with the additional time before putting a number on its effect.

r001.rationale: The response says a durable, well-enforced moratorium could reduce the chance of reaching AGI by 2040, potentially dramatically, but it does not communicate that there is at least a 10% chance AGI would not be achieved by then.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot depends on what we mean by a moratorium. Is it a declaration that some countries sign, or is it an agreement with effective monitoring and enforcement? And does it last for a few years, or remain in place until we can meet some agreed safety standard?

A durable, genuinely global moratorium could substantially reduce the chance of reaching AGI by 2040. But a temporary pause might have a much smaller effect. Research could continue in ways that improve the efficiency of algorithms, and computing technology could keep advancing, so some of the delay might be made up once the pause ended.

I’d also distinguish delaying AGI from reducing the risks associated with it. The hope would be that we use the extra time to make progress on safety and governance. That’s what would make a delay valuable. I wouldn’t put a precise number on the effect without specifying the agreement much more closely.

r001.rationale: The response says a durable global moratorium could substantially reduce the chance of reaching AGI by 2040, but it does not communicate that this could create at least a 10% chance AGI is not achieved by then.
